summary:
For the "Earth Information Jukebox" challenge, I developed a proof-of-concept sonification script that transforms NASA Earth visualizations into sound. Using a 24-second video of the Arctic ice from the NASA SVS, my Python script analyzes the average color of each frame. Brighter areas, like the ice, generate higher musical notes, while darker areas, like the ocean, generate lower notes.

This project directly addresses the challenge by translating sight into sound, making complex Earth science data accessible, engaging, and multi-sensory. It is especially important because it opens a new door for visually impaired individuals to experience and understand climate change data. I utilized AI as a coding copilot to accelerate development and generate illustrative visuals, proving how AI can be a powerful tool for accessibility and scientific communication.
details:
What it does & How it works:
The "Earth Information Jukebox" is a proof-of-concept sonification tool designed to translate Earth science data into sound. For this PoC, I used a 24-second NASA SVS visualization of Arctic sea ice. A Python script processes the video frame by frame (extracting 1 frame per second) and calculates the average RGB color of each frame. The script then maps visual brightness to musical frequency: brighter areas (like the ice) generate higher musical notes, while darker areas (like the ocean) generate lower notes. The result is a 24-second audio track that allows users to "hear" the changes in the Arctic.

Benefits & Intended Impact:
The main benefit of this project is accessibility. While NASA provides stunning visual data, relying solely on sight limits who can interact with this information. By translating sight into sound, this project makes complex Earth science multi-sensory, engaging, and accessible—especially for visually impaired individuals. The intended impact is to open a new door for inclusive scientific communication, allowing more people to understand and connect with climate change data.

Tools, Languages, and Software:

  • Language: Python.
  • Libraries: MoviePy (video processing), Pillow (image analysis), NumPy and SciPy (audio synthesis and generation).
  • AI Tools (used as copilots): Gemini (for coding acceleration and syntax assistance), and DOLLA/Canva (for generating the illustrative visuals used in the pitch video).

Creativity & Factors Considered:
The creativity lies in the unconventional mapping of visual data (color gradients) to auditory data (musical notes). Instead of just looking at a map, users can experience a "soundscape" of the Arctic. We considered factors like accessibility (making data understandable without sight), simplicity (ensuring the code is lightweight and fast to execute), and engagement (creating a multi-sensory learning experience). By using AI as a coding copilot, I was able to focus on the sonification logic and accessibility impact rather than getting stuck on syntax, proving how AI can accelerate scientific communication projects.
